newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's Aker probes options, including RGI merger.
newsitem.headline: Norway's Aker probes options, including RGI merger.

text.p: Norwegian offshore and building materials group Aker ASA said on Sunday it was probing various options for growth such as a merger with investment group RGI ASA, its largest shareholder.
But Aker spokesman Frode Geitvik declined to comment on media reports at the weekend that the company, one of Norway's biggest, was planning to propose a merger with RGI on Monday.

"We are considering various alternatives for Aker," he told Reuters. "One is a merger with RGI, but it is just one alternative. We are also studying the industry in general and we are looking into other investment possibilities."
Trawler-based RGI, or Research Group International, earlier this year acquired 30 percent of Aker shares and has options to buy nearly 10 percent more.
Geitvik denied a report by financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv that Aker planned to sell its 33 percent stake in cement company Scancem of Sweden's Skanska as part of a restructuring.
"This is wrong," he said. "We are not going to sell our share in Scancem. This is one of our key areas."
Aker's other key area is offshore. Shareholders in Aker ASA and Maritime Group ASA last week approved the merger of Aker's Oil and Gas Technology group and Maritime.

Norway's two main suppliers to the oil industry will merge to form a new company, Aker Maritime ASA. The deal is expected to be completed by the end of November, raising speculation among analysts that Aker would be reduced to a holding company.
Dagens Naeringsliv said a merger between Aker and RGI was imminent.

"The board of Aker is on standby," the article on Saturday said. "Early in the coming week, probably already on Monday, the board will meet to decide whether to recommend that merger talks with RGI begin. The plans have progressed to an extent where proposals have been made for the new company to be named RGI Aker."
"The merged company will get an annual turnover of more than 20 billion crowns as well as almost 20,000 employees."

It said Energy and Industry Minister Jens Stoltenberg was in favour of Aker and RGI joining forces. Major shareholders such as pension fund Folketrygdfondet and insurance company UNI Storebrand ASA had probably been informed of the idea of a quick merger, the article said.
RGI leader Kjell Inge Roekke was said to be ready to move back to Norway and register the investment group, which is now based in the Netherland Antilles.
Daily Finansavisen said a merger was the ultimate goal of RGI's aggressive purchase of Aker shares last spring.
